trivia_fact: The Trusted Platform Module (TPM) specification was created by the Trusted Computing Group, but Microsoft was the driving force — they needed hardware-backed security for BitLocker encryption. TPM 2.0 (2014) is now mandatory for Windows 11 and increasingly used in Linux for measured boot and disk encryption.

The Spectre and Meltdown vulnerabilities (2018) showed that CPU speculative execution could leak secrets across process boundaries. Patches cost 5-30% performance on some workloads. These hardware bugs proved that security cannot be purely a software concern and spawned an entire research field of transient execution attacks.

Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) are tamper-resistant devices that generate, store, and use cryptographic keys without ever exposing them. Every credit card transaction, TLS certificate authority, and cryptocurrency exchange depends on HSMs. They self-destruct (zeroize) keys if tampered with physically.

Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) creates encrypted memory enclaves that even the OS and hypervisor cannot read. Used for confidential computing — processing sensitive data without trusting the cloud provider. However, SGX has been attacked repeatedly (Plundervolt, SGAxe) and Intel deprecated it on consumer CPUs in 12th gen.

UEFI Secure Boot verifies that the bootloader is signed by a trusted key before executing it. It prevents bootkits and rootkits but initially caused Linux distribution headaches because Microsoft controlled the signing keys. Most distros now use a Microsoft-signed shim bootloader to chain-load their own signed GRUB.

topic_text: Row Hammer: RAM Reads as Attacks
trivia_fact: Repeatedly reading a DRAM row can flip bits in adjacent rows due to electrical interference. Researchers demonstrated using this to escalate privileges, escape VMs, and compromise browsers — all through memory reads. ECC memory mitigates but does not eliminate it. Modern DDR5 includes built-in row hammer protections.

YubiKey popularized hardware security keys for two-factor authentication. A single key supports FIDO2/WebAuthn, TOTP, PIV smart card, and OpenPGP. They have no battery, no Bluetooth, and are nearly impossible to phish because the key verifies the website's origin before responding. Google required all employees to use hardware keys in 2017 and eliminated phishing.

Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) exploit manufacturing variations in silicon to create unique identifiers for each chip — like a semiconductor fingerprint. No two chips, even from the same wafer, produce the same PUF output. Used for device authentication, key generation, and anti-counterfeiting in IoT and military hardware.

AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) encrypts each VM's memory with a unique key managed by a dedicated security processor. Even the hypervisor cannot read guest memory. This enables confidential computing in the cloud — AWS (Nitro Enclaves), Azure (Confidential VMs), and GCP all offer SEV-based instances.

Side-channel attacks extract secrets by observing physical signals: power consumption (differential power analysis), electromagnetic emissions, timing variations, and even acoustic emanations. Smart card PIN extraction via power analysis was demonstrated in the late 1990s. Modern hardware includes countermeasures like constant-time operations and power noise injection.
